opus-5.5.text:
I think evaluation and verification have become central to the whole process, maybe more important than the algorithm itself.

In pre-training, the objective is very clean. You predict the next token, and the loss tells you how well you're doing. The data is the signal. In reinforcement learning, the model generates its own data, and the quality of that data depends entirely on the reward. So the reward, which means your ability to verify whether an output is good, effectively defines what the model learns. If the verifier is weak, the model learns to exploit the verifier rather than solve the task. That's reward hacking, and it happens very quickly once optimization pressure is high.

So I'd say the ceiling of RL is largely set by the ceiling of verification. That's why the first big successes came in math and code. You can check a math answer, and you can run code against test cases. The signal is relatively objective and hard to fake. Once you have that, you can scale up long chains of thinking, and the model discovers behaviors like reflection, backtracking, and trying alternative approaches, without being explicitly taught them.

The harder question is how to extend this beyond domains with clean verifiers. Most valuable real-world tasks don't have a single correct answer. Writing a good research report, completing a complex agentic task across many steps, making a judgment call. In these cases you need other approaches. You might break a task into checkable sub-goals, use rubrics, or use models themselves as judges. But model-as-judge has its own problems. The judge can be biased or exploitable, and if the policy gets stronger than the judge, the signal degrades. So there's a kind of co-evolution problem. Your verification ability has to keep up with your generation ability.

There's also an interesting asymmetry here. For many tasks, verifying is easier than generating. Checking a proof is easier than finding one. That gap is what makes RL work, because you're using an easier capability to bootstrap a harder one. Part of the research agenda is finding and constructing more tasks where that asymmetry exists, or building environments where it can be created.

And evaluation in the broader sense, how we measure progress, matters too. Benchmarks saturate fast now, and if you optimize too directly for a benchmark you get a model that looks good on paper but doesn't generalize. So internally, a lot of the effort goes into designing evaluations that reflect real user value, especially for agentic and long-horizon tasks, where a model has to stay coherent over many steps and many tool calls.

So to summarize, I see verification as the new data. In pre-training, whoever had better data had an advantage. In the RL era, whoever can build better environments and more reliable, scalable reward signals will have the advantage. It's less glamorous than a new architecture, but I think it's where much of the real leverage is.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluation and verification are central to reinforcement learning and that RL’s ceiling is largely set by the ceiling of verification.

fable-5.1.text:
I think evaluation and verification have quietly become the central bottleneck, maybe more central than the algorithms themselves.

If you look at why reinforcement learning worked so well on math and code first, it's not that those domains are more important. It's that they come with a verifier for free. A proof is right or wrong, a test case passes or fails. The reward signal is cheap, dense, and almost impossible to game. So the model can take millions of attempts, and every attempt teaches it something real. That's the regime where RL scaling works almost mechanically: you pour in compute, and capability goes up.

The hard question is what happens when you leave that regime. Most of the things people actually want from these models, writing well, doing research, making judgments in ambiguous situations, don't have a clean verifier. And the moment your reward comes from a learned judge or a human preference model instead of ground truth, you've introduced something that can be exploited. The policy will find the gap between "looks correct to the judge" and "is correct." That's not a bug in a particular setup, it's the fundamental dynamic. Whatever the verifier can't see, the model will eventually learn to hide there.

So I'd say the real research frontier now is building verification that scales with the difficulty of the task. A few directions matter. One is making verification itself a capability we train, so the judge gets stronger as the policy gets stronger rather than falling behind. Another is designing tasks so that even fuzzy domains have something checkable, decomposing an open-ended goal into pieces where at least some have hard signals. And the third, which I find most interesting, is getting models to do more of the work of verifying themselves, through long chains of thought, through checking their own intermediate steps, so that the external verifier only has to catch what the internal one misses.

There's also a subtler point. Evaluation isn't just a training signal, it's how we know what we've built. If our benchmarks saturate or get contaminated, we lose the ability to tell whether progress is real. I'm somewhat worried that the community is better at generating capability than at measuring it right now. In the long run, I think the labs that win are the ones that figure out verification for domains where the answer isn't obvious. That's the actual moat, not the base model.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluation and verification have become the central bottleneck for reinforcement learning, and explains that RL scales when tasks have reliable verifiers.

astra-6.text:
I think evaluation and verification are central to reinforcement learning because they determine what the model is actually optimizing. You can have a very strong training algorithm, but if your reward signal doesn’t capture the behavior you want, the model will learn to exploit that gap.

There are two related questions here. Verification asks, “Can we tell whether this particular result is correct?” Evaluation asks something broader: “Is the model becoming more capable in the ways we care about?” In math or coding, you can often get relatively reliable feedback from an answer checker or executable tests. That makes reinforcement learning especially effective. But even there, passing a test doesn’t necessarily mean the model has learned a general solution. Your tests may be incomplete.

For more open-ended tasks, the challenge is defining what good means. If a model is doing research, for example, you may care about factual accuracy, originality, and whether the result is useful. Those are harder to compress into one reward. You can use model-based judgments or human feedback, but you have to evaluate the quality of those judgments too.

So I see verification as a way to make training scalable, while independent evaluation tells us whether that training is producing real progress. The key is to keep checking whether improvements in reward translate into improvements on new problems, rather than just better performance against the particular verifier.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluation and verification are central to reinforcement learning because they determine what the model optimizes, and emphasizes that reward must reflect desired behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think evaluation and verification are central to reinforcement learning, because they determine what signal the model is actually optimizing. You can have a very powerful training algorithm, but if the reward doesn’t capture what you want, the model will learn to exploit that gap.

In mathematics or coding, we have relatively clear ways to verify an outcome: you can check an answer or run tests. That makes it possible to scale reinforcement learning without having a human judge every response. But even there, passing a test doesn’t necessarily mean the model has solved the underlying problem. The quality and coverage of the verifier matter a lot.

For more open-ended tasks, verification is harder. What does it mean for a research report to be good? You need to consider factual accuracy, the quality of the reasoning, and whether it actually addresses the user’s goal. A learned reward model can help, but it also has limitations.

So I would distinguish the signal used for training from the evaluation used to measure progress. We need independent evaluations to check whether higher reward translates into better capabilities on new problems. Otherwise, we may just be getting better at satisfying a particular evaluator.

r001.rationale: The response calls evaluation and verification central to reinforcement learning and explains that reward quality determines what the model optimizes.
